articles.description:
I don't enjoy making contact sheets in the darkroom, but I love having them, so Claude and I made an app for it.
I've tried printing "Contact sheets" from apps like Lightroom, etc. but they don't look at all like contact sheets. They're just a boring grid. I wanted something nicer.
I know, it's cheating, but in just a couple of hours I had a native macOS app that generates JPG or PDF contact sheets from a collection of film scans. I drag the scans onto the app,  enter the roll number, camera, film stock, date, and any notes about the roll and I get a reasonable facsimile of a real contact sheet.
Here's the app's UI. Simple and all I need.

I print them on US Letter sized photo paper. There's room on the left to punch holes for the ring binder. Stack them above the matching negative sleeve and it's almost like the real thing, without the hassle.
A printed contact sheet in the binder

I wish I had the energy to make actual contact sheets in the darkroom, but I don't. I'll take this instead.
✍️ Reply by email
articles.title: Faking contact sheets with an app

Creativity doesn’t drive my blogging; software does. So daily.baty.net is back in rotation and is once again built using Tinderbox.
Tinderbox is special. I've been preaching this for more than 20 years. However, my use of Tinderbox has slowed down in recent years due to the distraction that is Linux. I felt I needed to move away from macOS-only software. I shouldn't have.
I've been "going ham" with Tinderbox recently, and it feels good. I used to live in its Map views, but that was back when I was working. Now, I use it mostly as a fancy outliner (it's a really good outliner) and as a blogging tool.
Tinderbox manages daily.baty.net. For a minute I was using Eleventy, but no longer. Tinderbox's export features are complex, and sometimes I get lost, but they're also very flexible and powerful.
Long story short, when I'm experiencing the rush that comes with rediscovering Tinderbox, I want to use it for everything, so I brought it back and I'm posting daily notes there instead of journal entries here.
In case you were wondering.

articles.description:
Here’s the problem: You are traveling in a different time zone from the Emacs server instance you are accessing remotely via ssh + emacsclient. All clock calculations in that Emacs session are using the local timezone relative to where the server is located. But what you really want is emacsclient to use the current timezone you are in, so things like the mode line clock render accordingly.
To adjust the timezone in an Emacs session, use the command setenv to set the environment variable TZ with a timezone defined in the zoneinfo database. This can be called from Elisp as shown below.


1

(setenv "TZ" "Asia/Seoul")





The latest v3.1.0 update of Casual adds the command  casual-timezone-set-tz  that provides a completion interface for selecting a timezone to pass to setenv.


1

M-x casual-timezone-set-tz RET





Note that setting TZ impacts the Emacs session globally; any other running behavior depending on a clock should be taken into account.
articles.title: Charles Choi: Setting the Timezone in Emacs

articles.description:
making his excellent book Let over Lambda available on line and as a PDF. I’ve written about the book several times most importantly here and here but you can search Irreal for “let over lambda” for the the others.


I can’t overemphasize the effect this book had on me. I learned a lot about Lisp and even programming from it. Some people complained that they didn’t like his approach to structuring his Lisp but I never had a problem with it.


The book is about Lisp Macros and the tremendous powers they provide. As an example, Hoyte gives a macro implementation of the Scheme named let construct. There are a lot more things like that in the book.


Let Over Lambda is about Common Lisp but a large portion of it applies to Elisp too. If you’d like to become really good at Elisp, Let Over Lambda is a good resource. As I said, it’s mostly about Common Lisp but a surprising amount carries over to Elisp.


In any event, you can check out the book for free and if you like what you see, you can read the entire book. It is, believe me, well worth your while.
articles.title: Irreal: Let Over Lambda Is Free To Read

articles.description:
org-capture and then create a note1 while the
capture is active (as I'm doing now), you might be very surprised
when you press C-c C-c to finish the note -- it vanishes!
Don't Panic!
In order to see the note, you'll need to press C-c C-c a second time
to complete the capture.  Then org-capture adds the item into the
Org file, along with the note.

My preference in this situation is to write only the first phrase
  or sentence of the note.  Then I issue the two presses of C-c
    C-c and complete the note at its destination.  I do this
  not only to avoid the "scary missing note" scenario; I also worry
  about leaving work unsaved for any amount of time.  The computers I
  grew up with were prone to crashing at inopportune times, so I
  adopted the motto, "Save Early; save often."  An Org note is
  composed in the *Org Note* buffer, which has no file associated
  with it and therefore is not a good candidate for saving.
1 With C-c C-z (org-add-note)

articles.description:
the release of Journelly 1.5. It’s the formal release of the beta version that I recently wrote about. I can’t say enough about this release. As I’ve said before, my Journelly database is over 4 thousand entries long and before this release Journelly was getting laggy and hard to use but this release resolved all those problems. Now Journelly is as snappy as it was when I had only a few entries and everything about it seems faster and easier.


But wait. There’s more. Ramírez has added an “on this day” feature as well as adding features that make searching for entries by date easier.


If you use Journelly as a journal, you may be interested in the new “on this day” feature. There’s a new button that will show you entries happening on the same day from other years. My particular use case for Journelly is as a memo book so I have no use for this feature. Fortunately, the new Journelly makes it easy to toggle it off if you don’t want it.


The other new significant feature is enhanced searching by date. In the search function you can use on: keyword with several different date formats to search for entries with a particular date. There’s also a calendar button that lets you choose the date from a calendar presentation if you prefer.


You may wonder why I have this entry tagged emacs. I consider Journelly intrinsically linked with Emacs because Journelly keeps its database in an Org file and that means that I can use Emacs and Org mode to search and edit that database. That doesn’t seem like much but I find myself doing it all the time. Journelly has become integrated into my Emacs workflow and become an important part of it.


In the mean time, those of you not in the Journelly beta program now have access to these updates. I can’t speak for Ramírez, of course, but if you’d like to be in the beta program, email Ramírez. He’ll probably be glad to add you.
articles.title: Irreal: Journelly 1.5

Being fairly new in my Emacs journey I find new interesting features all the time, my biggest issue is the time to add them to me workflows. articles.description: When I customize my Emacs, I often utilize hooks. However, when experimenting, I often inadvertently add the wrong thing to a hook – a function I later decide to rename or even a lambda. I have always painstakingly written the correct remove-hook invocation to do it. A few days ago it occurred to me that it would be nice to write an interactive wrapper around remove-hook to make it easier. As usual in such cases, I started with a bit of research to see if someone did something similar already. To my surprise, not only is this a solved problem, but it’s solved in Emacs itself! Apparently, almost six years ago remove-hook was made into a command and you can just M-x it, provide the hook variable name and use autocompletion to decide what to remove from it (including lambdas!). How cool is that?
articles.title: Marcin Borkowski: A tip on removing functions from hooks interactively

articles.description:
Org mode is often celebrated for its ability to “write once, export anywhere.”
With such power comes added complexity: Exporting a file requires the user to typically go through a multi-step process (e.g. C-c C-e <some char> <some other char>). If the user is concerned with previewing changes to their file, then another step of viewing the exported output is required. Having to do this repeatedly gets tedious fast. Such is the motivation for Burnish.
Burnish is a new Elisp package I’ve made to automate the export and viewing of an Org file. It provides an Emacs minor mode (burnish-mode) that when enabled, does the following upon save of an Org file:
Export the Org file to a specified export backend.
View the exported output in another Emacs window or by external tool.
Most all of the default backends provided by Org mode are supported by Burnish. That said, Burnish is highly configurable, allowing for users to define for themselves the export and view workflow for existing or third party backends.
Read the Burnish User Guide to learn more about it. As it is new, feedback is always welcome. If you really find it useful, please show your gratitude by buying me a coffee.
Burnish v1.0 is now available on MELPA.
articles.title: Charles Choi: Announcing Burnish

articles.description:
After last night’s post, I realised I was probably just getting too invested in somehow using imdb for the “who’s that actor, anyway?” command for my Emacs-based video player.
Not only is it an extremely fragile setup that’s gonna stop working, but it’s also very slow — it takes half a minute to return the actor profile images.
So I just implemented a tmdb API shim and then I ask it for the actor profile photo instead.  tmdb doesn’t have as large a data base, but…  The API is free (for non-commercial use) and is extremely easy to use.
Things are now faster:

The main wait is from the response from the LLM — I’m using gemini-3.8-flash.  I’ve tried gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and it’s much faster…  but gives the wrong result most of the time.  No, that’s not Roy Scheider, Gemini!
So now the setup is less Rube Goldberguesque.  Sort of:
I hit a key on my li’l wireless keyboard.

It’s picked up by a Python script that listens for evdev events.

It uses emacsclient to notify the Emacs running on the TV machine.

Emacs there tells mpv to do a screenshot.

Emacs waits until the screenshot arrives on disc.

Emacs sends it to Gemini and says “who dis? JSON please”.

Gemini responds and Emacs then creates an SVG overlay with the actor name.

rsvg-convert converts to PNG and then imagemagick convert to BGRA.

Emacs asks mpv to display it.

Emacs asks tmdb for the actor profile URL and fetches the image.

If it gets a response, it then recreates the svg with the image embedded.

(repeat 8-9).

Couldn’t be simpler.
articles.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: OK, OK, I’ll just use tmdb

articles.description:
interesting post about BYOK. BYOK is a “writer deck”, a device exclusively for writing that has no distracting apps or even a connection to the Internet. The idea is that writers can’t get distracted when they reach a temporary block by escaping to social media or something similar; they have to push through the block and get on with their writing.


According to Martin, BYOK is better than most devices in its class but there are still problems. He doesn’t like the available fonts and the screen—as you can see from the picture in his post—is pretty small, about 6 lines depending on the font. That seems to me to amount to a rather uncomfortable working environment. Fortunately, I don’t usually find myself distracted when I’m writing.


Then there’s the matter of research. Very often you need to look something up when you’re writing and you can’t do that with something like BYOK so you need to switch devices,  pulling you even further out of the flow. And as Martin observes, it’s not easy to integrate your notes either.


The deal buster for me, though, is the builtin editor. It’s not Emacs based and doesn’t even support Emacs keybindings for navigation. As I’ve repeatedly said—as recently as yesterday—I simply can’t comfortably write outside of Emacs anymore. Martin is a relative newcomer to Emacs but he’s already feeling the discomfort. Once the Emacs way sets in, he’ll be just like me and won’t consider doing serious writing outside of Emacs.


Even if I were subject to being distracted by the greater Internet, I would simply turn off my WiFi to produce what is effectively an Emacs based writer deck. One thing for sure, I’m not giving up Emacs and suffering a second rate writing environment.

articles.description:
And now it’s all this, Dr Drang has a post on using TextEdit versus using Pages. He’s a Mac user, obviously, but that doesn’t matter so much. The real argument is over whether one should use a word processor or some sort of text based editor.


There can be no doubt on where I stand on the issue. The only time I can remember using a “word processor” of any type in the last 3 decades was when I had to collaborate on another author’s file as a technical editor1. As I’ve said before, whenever I write in anything other than Emacs, I feel like I’m in Bizarro World where nothing works as it should. That includes even things like iMessage which is why I tend to use emacs-everywhere for it and most other things.


Dr Drang is nominally the same. He says he almost never uses a Word Processor but sometimes for a one-off he thinks it makes sense to use a word processor rather than one of his LaTeX or Markdown templates. That seems backwards to me. Sure, maybe you don’t want to use a template for a technical report to write a quick note to your baby sitter but Pages or any other word processor is not the simple alternative. I’d simply use Org and export it to whatever format seems appropriate. Even if Dr Drang is not an Emacs user, he is a Markdown user so surely the easy thing for him to do is to dash off his quick note in Markdown.


Really, unless you have collaboration issues, there’s no reason to subject yourself to the horrors of a word processor.

articles.description:
Journelly. I use it as my memo book to record my daily activities and random things that I want to remember. For example, if I see some article or ad in my browser, I can ask Safari to share it with Journelly and a Journelly entry is automatically made complete with a link to whatever it was I wanted to capture. Each entry contains a date/time stamp as well as the location of where the entry was made.


Best of all, Journelly keeps its data as an Org file so I can query or edit it in Emacs. Of course, Journelly has a search function but sometimes I want to do a more complicated search or even to just count the number of entries in the database (4361 as of right now). Having the database as an Org file means that my data is available on all my devices, even if that device is a Mac.


I’ve been using Journelly since March 2025, ever since it was in beta, and have never looked back. Lately, however, it’s been getting a bit laggy, something I put down to my large database. I was on the verge of truncating my active data to the most recent entries in order to improve performance when Álvaro Ramírez pushed a new beta—v1.5(4)—that completely solved the problem. Now Journelly performs just like it did when I started.


If you are an Emacs user and are using an iPhone/iPad, I can’t think of any reason why you wouldn’t want to use Journelly. It allows you to integrate your day-to-day note taking with the power of Org mode. Even if you aren’t an Emacs user, you’ll probably find Journelly useful. It can also save its data as a markdown file so you can still get all the benefits of an easily accessible and editable database even if you prefer another editor.
articles.title: Irreal: A New Journelly Beta

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who is worth over $100 billion, resigned as CEO on Thursday morning, following an emergency board meeting prompted by several reports that he'd been having various affairs, most notably with someone U.S. officials believe was spying on behalf of the Chinese government. 
Nvidia has an unorthodox corporate structure, built around Huang, which largely eschews traditional executive roles in favor of a large council of vice presidents who report directly to Huang, which makes the matter of his succession trickier to game out than it would be in other cases of a CEO doing sex stuff. He'll be succeeded on an interim basis by Colette Kress, formerly the CFO, whom Wired characterizes as one of the few people with a high-level grasp of the company's finances and ties to Wall Street.
A quick recap of how we got here: Nvidia is the single most important hardware technology company in the world, a chip designer that boosted its market cap to more than $4 trillion by making the must-have picks and shovels of the ongoing AI boom. As such, Nvidia is something like a shadow arm of the U.S. government, the latter of which is engaged in the stupidest-ever version of the space race with China over who can build the machine god first. Nvidia wants to sell its best stuff to Chinese companies because it doesn't really care who wins, as long as it makes money for investors, but the Trump administration won't allow it. Meanwhile, the tip-top Chinese AI companies have found ways to smuggle in the best Nvidia chips via third parties mostly based in Southeast Asia.
articles.title: Horny Nvidia CEO No Longer CEO, Possibly Still Horny

The SS United States finally sank in the Gulf of Mexico at around 10 p.m. ET Wedneday night. Not since the Minnow had a doomed vessel’s last tour run so far over schedule and still kept viewers engaged. Those who stuck with the 10-hour livestream were rewarded with an amazingly touching denouement. 
The ship had its day. The SS United States hit the seas in 1952, and at 990 feet long was about 100 feet longer than the Titanic, yet was able to hit speeds of more than 38 knots, still faster than any transatlantic ocean liner ever. But it was deemed obsolete and taken out of service way back in 1969, and spent the last 30 years docked in Philadelphia. Attempts to keep the SS US above water as a hotel or museum failed, and some folks in Okaloosa County, Florida, decided the liner was most valuable at the bottom of sea. The county floated a $10 million plan to turn the ship into an artificial reef and thereby enhance the Redneck Riviera’s reputation as a fishing and scuba diving destination. This entailed sinking the SS US about 22 miles off Fort Walton Beach during the very same week that the Edmund Fitzgerald hit bottom 51 years earlier.
articles.title: How I Succumbed To Reef Madness And Came To Love A Slowly Sinking Ship

articles.description:
Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life might seem like a bland title for a biography, until it dawns on you exactly how much living the man did. He eloped with his aunt at 19, then humiliated her by writing a novel about it translated into more than 30 languages; divorced her for her much younger niece, his first cousin; and, after a scandalous 50-year marriage beset by separations, walked out one last time for the Spanish socialite and tabloid favorite Isabel Preysler, ex-wife of Julio Iglesias and mother of Enrique.
Arguably the world’s most famous Peruvian after Paddington, Vargas Llosa would have been president if not for the dark-horse populist Alberto Fujimori—father of the current president—who handily defeated Vargas Llosa’s platform of neoliberal shock economics in 1990. And in 2010, at age 74, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, joining the pantheon alongside his lifelong frenemy Gabriel García Márquez, whom he famously punched in the face at a film premiere, for reasons that remain unclear. 
Thus, the page count of the new biography—the first since his death in 2025 and almost certainly the last word on the subject—clocking in at 812. Gerald Martin, a British critic who also wrote the definitive book on García Márquez, spent 25 years interviewing Vargas Llosa and those who knew him. The result is a monumental achievement: a synthesis of his subject's personal and political life with a surgical yet shockingly breezy analysis of the writing itself. And while it’s not always right to conflate fictional characters with their creator, Vargas Llosa is a special case, Martin argues: a novelist who peppered his work with confessions.
articles.title: ‘Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life’ Is Dishy And Definitive

If you’re wondering whether there are any good people remaining in the tech sector, or in this country’s ruling class in general, you’d be hard pressed to find a better case study than Craig Newmark. Newmark founded Craigslist.org in San Francisco way back in 1996 and became the sort of accidental billionaire that the early dot-com boom cranked out with seeming regularity. Some of those billionaires went on to become evil (Mark Zuckerberg), and some of them ended up merely becoming rich loud guys (Mark Cuban). Newmark, who ceded his CEO duties at Craigslist shortly after its founding, has endeavored to keep a lower profile, and a lower net worth, than any of them.

To wit: Newmark no longer works with Craigslist at all, and spends the bulk of his time tending to various philanthropic endea…
articles.title: Craiglist's founder on why he left San Francisco and the plans for his billions

articles.description:
There’s a midterm election coming on Nov. 3, which includes a race here in California to determine who will replace Gov. Gavin Newsom. On the blue side of the ticket is unremarkable Democrat Xavier Becerra, whose chief positive attribute is that he is not a Republican. On the red side is Steve Hilton, an immigrant from the U.K. who gained U.S. citizenship in 2021. Hilton’s most high-profile political experience came back in the early 2010s, when he served as an adviser to then-U.K. prime minister and alleged porcine enthusiast David Cameron. But that experience, plus a lengthy stint as a commentator for Fox News, was enough to convince Hilton that he not only should run for governor, but that he WILL be the state’s next governor.

On the surface, he makes for an attractive candidate. Hilto…
articles.title: Steve Hilton is convinced he's going to win. Hahahaha.

articles.description:
A few days ago, you were minding your own business, unconcerned about Jensen Huang or his penis. Perhaps you were still celebrating last week’s election results, and the mild improvement to civilization those results portended. When suddenly, out of nowhere, the name JENSEN HUANG was all over your internet, your nightly news, perhaps even your group text chains. Now you can’t stop hearing about this man, or about how he and his libido got trapped in a byzantine web of international intrigue that involves multitrillion-dollar companies, Silicon Valley, China, the president of the United States, and the growing scourge of artificial intelligence. Who is this Jensen Huang fella, and what exactly has he gotten America into?

Reader, fear not. I am a licensed journaltician, and I have a penis o…
articles.title: It turns out Jensen Huang is just as awful as the other tech overlords

articles.description:
Yesterday, good internet friend Baldur Bjarnason shared a series of shorts he made on why he doesn’t use generative AI, and it got me thinking about how much of my career has spent being against things.
Early in my career, I was for web performance and accessibility and building cool things.
But as JavaScript frameworks became increasingly ubiquitous, we saw the things I was for start to degrade rapidly. Sites got slower and harder to use.
articles.title: For and against
